items.title: The square root of 2 cannot be written as a fraction
items.claim: Diagonal of a unit square has length root 2. The Pythagoreans believed all lengths were ratios of whole numbers. Hippasus showed root 2 wasn't. Legend says the Pythagoreans drowned him for revealing it.
items.prompt: Sketch the proof that root 2 is irrational.

options.text: It has too many decimal places

Assume root 2 = a/b in lowest terms. Then 2b squared = a squared, so a is even (say a = 2c). Then 2b squared = 4c squared, so b squared = 2c squared, so b is even. But a and b were lowest terms — contradiction
Because computers can't store it exactly

items.reveal:
The Pythagorean brotherhood (c. 500 BC) believed numbers were the foundation of reality and that all measurable lengths could be expressed as ratios of integers.

Hippasus of Metapontum supposedly proved the diagonal of a square is not commensurable with its side. Different ancient sources say he drowned at sea — some say by accident, some say murdered by his fellow Pythagoreans for exposing the result.

The proof: suppose root 2 equals a/b in lowest terms. Squaring: 2 = a squared over b squared, so 2 b squared equals a squared. Hence a squared is even, so a is even (say a = 2c). Substituting: 2 b squared = 4 c squared, so b squared = 2 c squared, so b squared is even, so b is even. Both a and b are even — contradiction with 'lowest terms'.

The discovery that not all numbers are rational was a major shock; the Greeks came to call these new quantities 'incommensurable'. Modern mathematics calls them irrationals — and there are vastly more of them than rationals.
items.why: Numbers feel like they should always be expressible as ratios. The very first geometric constructions reveal they're not.

items.title: Ice cream sales correlate with drownings — neither causes the other
items.claim: When ice cream sales rise, drowning deaths rise. Strong correlation. Both peak in summer. Neither causes the other — they share a common cause (hot weather drives both ice cream consumption and swimming).
items.prompt: What's wrong with inferring causation from correlation?

options.text: Correlation can arise from: X causes Y; Y causes X; both have a common cause (confounder); selection bias; chance. Without further evidence (experiment or careful causal modelling), we cannot distinguish which
Causation always implies correlation, so causation and correlation are the same

items.reveal_title: Hill criteria, confounders, and the structure of causal inference
items.reveal:
Correlation = statistical association. Causation = mechanistic dependence.

Reasons for correlation without direct causation:
- Common cause (confounder): heat causes both ice cream sales and drownings.
- Reverse causation: rooster crowing 'causes' the sun to rise? Actually opposite.
- Selection bias: hospitalised patients show that brain injury and dietary habits correlate, but only because they were both selected by the hospital criteria.
- Coincidence: with enough variables, spurious correlations are inevitable (https://tylervigen.com/spurious-correlations).

Establishing causation usually requires:
1. Randomised controlled experiment: randomly assign causes, observe effects. Eliminates confounders by design.
2. Natural experiments: variation in cause that's plausibly random (timing of policy changes, weather).
3. Bradford Hill criteria (1965): strength, consistency, specificity, temporality, biological gradient, plausibility, coherence, experiment, analogy. Used in epidemiology when RCTs aren't possible.
4. Causal inference frameworks (Pearl's directed acyclic graphs, potential outcomes).

Famous miscalls:
- Hormone replacement therapy and heart disease (observational said 'protective'; RCT said 'harmful').
- Vitamin E and cancer prevention (observational said 'protective'; RCT said 'no effect').
- Coffee and heart disease (many flip-flops).

The replication crisis in psychology and biomedicine partly reflects systematic overinterpretation of correlation as causation.

When RCTs aren't possible (ethics, scale), causal inference is harder but not impossible — but requires careful design and explicit assumption-naming.
items.why: 'Correlation implies causation' is a famous fallacy — but the converse fallacy ('all correlations are meaningless') is also wrong. Understanding the structure of causal evidence is key to scientific literacy.

items.title: A skydiver and a feather hit terminal velocity at hugely different speeds — but the math is the same
items.claim: Drop a steel ball: terminal velocity ~150 m/s. Drop a person: ~50 m/s. Drop a feather: ~1 m/s. All fall under the same gravity. The differences come from one equation: weight equals drag.

options.text: Terminal velocity is where gravitational force (mg, downward) exactly balances drag force (proportional to v squared for high speeds, or v for low speeds); the equilibrium speed depends on mass, cross-sectional area, drag coefficient and air density
Only on the height of the fall
Drag is the same for all objects

items.reveal_title: The drag equation and limit velocities
items.reveal:
For an object falling through air, two forces:
- Gravity: mg, downward.
- Drag: at high speed, F_drag = (1/2) * rho * v^2 * C_d * A, where rho is air density, C_d is drag coefficient, A is cross-sectional area.

At terminal velocity, drag equals gravity: v_terminal = sqrt(2 * m * g / (rho * C_d * A)).

Approximate terminal velocities:
- Steel ball (cm-scale): ~150 m/s.
- Skydiver in spread-eagle: ~50 m/s.
- Skydiver in head-first dive: ~90 m/s.
- Tennis ball: ~30 m/s.
- Raindrop (1mm): ~6.5 m/s.
- Snowflake: ~0.5-1 m/s.
- Dust mote: micrometres per second.

The famous 'Galileo dropped balls from the leaning tower of Pisa' demonstrates that g is the same for all masses — but only in vacuum. In air, lighter objects with high surface area to mass ratio fall slower because of drag.

Apollo 15 (1971): astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a feather on the lunar surface (no atmosphere). They hit the ground simultaneously — Galileo confirmed live on Earth television.

Felix Baumgartner (Red Bull Stratos jump, 2012) reached supersonic terminal velocity (~377 m/s) by jumping from the stratosphere where air is thinner. He broke the sound barrier with his body.
items.why: Galileo showed all objects fall the same — in vacuum. In air, drag dominates within seconds and terminal velocity is set by an unfamiliar combination of properties. The intuition only holds in idealised conditions.
